## Misleading “tough” and the old blueprint
Students’ definitions of toughness cluster around grit, stoicism/“playing through pain,” showing “no signs of distress,” and perseverance, implying an “inner warrior” who overcomes adversity through discipline while controlling outward emotion. The chapter argues this common picture is fundamentally wrong, and it traces the confusion across coaching, parenting, and “tough guys.”

## Bobby Knight: results-backed toughness defined by fear and control
Bobby Knight’s success (900+ wins; 3 NCAA championships; Final Four five times; especially the 1976 Indiana perfect season with a win over Michigan) supports his own link between outcomes and toughness: “That was a team that was almost impossible to beat, because of its toughness, its strength, its size,” and “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” His disciplined man-to-man press and defense exemplify the performance side.

Yet the chapter says Knight’s operational method is abusive: locker-room “tampons” for players he deemed “soft,” frequent cussing, accusations that he ordered managers to tape pictures of women’s genitalia in players’ rooms, a 1991 tirade (“This is absolute fucking bullshit… Now I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground… you will goddamn pay for it…”), toilet paper “covered in shit” to shame players, and physical abuse captured on video (including choking a player at practice). This is presented as toughness defined by showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear/authority/control.

## Authoritarian parenting: demandingness without responsiveness
The chapter generalizes the model with Baumrind’s two axes: **responsiveness** (attuned/supportive/acquiescent to children’s special needs and demands) and **demandingness** (maturity expectations, supervision, discipline, confronting disobedience). The “authoritarian” style is high demandingness/low responsiveness: parents rely on fear, threats, and punishment (e.g., “You need to do (this) because I said so”). A study of over one thousand parents found only **31%** of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally,” framing motivation as “about the sticks, not the carrots.” The chapter adds cultural persistence: a study where **81%** of Americans thought parents were too soft.

It stresses the caveat that punishment/expectations aren’t inherently wrong; problems arise when demand outweighs support, because “toughness” becomes control rather than help.

## Callousness and machismo: toughness as rationalized harm
The chapter defines **callous** as hardening, becoming insensitive, and developing a “thick skin,” then shows how “tough” language (“soft,” “hardening up,” “show no signs of weakness”) converts into narratives that rationalize harm: thick-skin stoicism, revenge stories (Karate Kid), and youth-sports routines framed as “testing” (running laps/burpees). Mark Hyman’s **Until It Hurts** is cited for youth clubs with frequent throwing up after workouts, insult-laden tirades, and the justification for pushing **eleven-year-olds** “until they puke”: “The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.”

Toughness is also tied to masculinity/machismo (“man up,” “There’s no crying in baseball!”; “stop being a pussy”), and the chapter claims research shows women handle pain quietly better, using this to question external machismo displays as “weakness.”

## Maryland fallout: pushing through danger fails (and can kill)
The chapter grounds consequences in the **May 29, 2018** University of Maryland conditioning workout with **ten 110-yard sprints**. By sprint **seven**, **Jordan McNair (19)** showed “profound fatigue,” reportedly bending over with cramps. The chapter argues this was bodily “protesting…screaming for help,” while coaches/trainers allegedly goaded him (e.g., “get him the [expletive] up,” “drag his [expletive] across the field”). After his final sprint, video shows him near-walking pace; after he complained of cramps, it took trainers **34 minutes** to remove him and **another 28 minutes** to call **911**; **one hour and 28 minutes** elapsed between his final sprint and ambulance transport. He died two weeks later from heatstroke, attributed “thanks in part to a horrid medical response,” and also to inability to distinguish pushing through pain from actual danger.

The chapter connects this to a broader trend of “extreme workouts” meant to “toughen up,” including **rhabdomyolysis (“rhabdo”)**: damaged muscle products leak into the bloodstream, increasing kidney demands; death can occur. It claims rhabdo shifted from once-rare causes (infections/drug use) toward more common cases due to extreme workouts, naming push-ups, squats, and burpees used to “test” athletes. Ohio University professor **B. David Ridpath** is quoted: strength coaches “often will ‘condition’ these players with a vengeance and a mandate to make them suffer.”

## Psychological consequences: dependence, fragility, and fear of failure
Research parallels are presented across parenting, sport, and military contexts: authoritarian parenting correlates with lower independence, more aggressive behavior, higher risky/substance behaviors; and in sport authoritarian demandingness links to lower grit, higher emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In the Israeli military, those raised in authoritarian environments reportedly coped worse than those raised in nurturing ones, described as “an appearance of discipline without true discipline.” Another study of **over 1,200** parents finds authoritarian parenting linked to higher child misbehavior.

Mechanistically, fear-based discipline produces dependence: obedience learned via fear leads adults to rely on fear-based motivation. An athlete quote describes punishment-by-exercise: coaches want you to “become stronger,” but it “gets in your head” so you work to avoid punishment.

## Redefining toughness: discomfort navigation, not control
The chapter’s through-line is that callous toughness trains people to respond to fear/power by maintaining a facade (“I’m not afraid of anything!”) and bashing through adversity; removing fear/power/control removes the needed skill for navigating adversity. It distinguishes **fake toughness** (control- and power-driven; developed through fear; fueled by insecurity; appearance over substance) from **real toughness** (a decision model under discomfort). Fake examples are repeatedly listed: Knight tantrums; “power without substance”; fighting/ass-kicking; gym bullies/message-board hard-asses; executives yelling; and coaches/parents confusing demandingness and control with respect.

The chapter states its maxim explicitly: **“Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”**

## Pete Carroll and science-backed coaching as contrast
Pete Carroll is offered as counterpoint: not “a saint,” but a coach who after being fired in the 1990s stopped imitating others and followed his own path, achieving rare success (one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl). The chapter attributes to him a toughness rooted in inner drive to stay focused, embrace challenges, bounce back, perseverance, and passion, with practices like “always compete,” paired with teaching skills to handle adversity.

The shift is mapped as control → autonomy; appearance → substance; rigid push → flexibility; fear motivation → inner drive; insecurity → “quiet confidence.” The chapter cites multiple successful coaches (Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy; John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D’Antoni with “We keep it positive here”) and Ken Reed’s summary: society assumes autocratic coaches are better because “It’s a myth. But it’s a vicious cycle.”

Science is cited via a **2008 Eastern Washington** study of ~**two hundred** basketball players/coaches: “keys” to mental toughness do not lie in autocratic/authoritarian/oppressive style; they appear in environments emphasizing **trust and inclusion, humility, and service**.

## Running as the “laboratory”: VCD replaces pushing with regulation
The author uses the Don Bowden Mile (seven men: six UC Berkeley; the author from University of Houston; **1,609 meters**) to demonstrate toughness under discomfort. Tactics include near-front placement early, gaze-lock behind “designated rabbits,” zoning out initially (“No one wins the race in the first half… they only lose it”), then reengaging near the end; each runner’s fatigue “signature” reveals breaking points.

At about **900 meters**, the author’s neck tightens/strains with a strange breath (almost a high-pitched gasp). Internal alarm triggers doubts (“This is too soon… You’re done”); after less than **100 meters** left, the voice becomes panic: “I can’t breathe. What the hell!? I can’t breathe!” He pulls off and collapses; then the sensation disappears after panic. The prior “pushing until you puked” toughness backfires, requiring a new tactic: relax and keep breathing/neck/mind steady at peak discomfort and doubt.

After a year+ of tests (scopes, echocardiograms, treadmill/biking to exhaustion), allergist **Dr. Stephen Miles** diagnoses **paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)**. Mechanism: vocal cords open on inhalation and partially close on exhalation, with a protective shutdown; in VCD, vocal cords “shut when they are supposed to open,” essentially blocking airways on inhalation, due to hyperresponsive cords ready to shut. Severe cases include inability-to-inhale sensation plus panic/fear/anxiety, which worsens symptoms. Triggers (American Thoracic Society): “strong emotions” and stress; other researchers emphasize hyperresponsive larynx and nervous system activity shifts priming cord closure in response to psychological or physical irritants.

## Scope and preview: lessons generalize beyond sport
Running anchors the discussion because it is solitary and “alone, in your head,” with immense discomfort, but lessons are presented as applicable to parenting, grief, and leading (six or sixty years old). The chapter closes by previewing four pillars: **(1) Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality; (2) Listen to Your Body; (3) Respond Instead of React; (4) Transcend Discomfort**, framed as “where we went off track” and why people persist in a control/fear facade model.

Bobby Knight’s résumé spans five decades and three universities: over nine hundred wins (third all-time in college basketball), five Final Fours, and three NCAA championships. His 1976 Indiana team won the NCAA tournament, including a win over Michigan for a perfect season, and Knight later attributed its edge to “toughness, its strength, its size.” He also defined toughness as “Being able to overcome obstacles. The “old model” is summarized as: Bobby Knight school of authoritarian coaching, authoritarian parenting, and callous leadership.

David Ridpath: these are not conditioning—“Taking a cue from a head coach with a desire to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots, the strength coach often will ‘condition’ these players with a vengeance and a mandate to make them suffer.”

He includes a quoted athlete response: “Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger. . . . It gets in your head and you start thinking, ‘I need to do better. I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished.”

Magness argues old-school toughness teaches people to respond to fear and power. The “hammer” metaphor: the body/mind are controlled via external pressure, facade (“I’m not afraid of anything!”) rather than managing real difficulty. Remove fear/power/control and the person lacks needed skills.

He labels this “fake toughness” as: control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and “based on appearance over substance.” He lists examples: Knight’s tantrums under “discipline”; power without substance; fighting/“ass-kicking”; gym bullies and message-board hard-asses; execs masking insecurity by yelling; strength coaches working athletes so hard they get injured/sick; “hating the ‘other’”; parents equating demandingness with discipline; coaches who mistake control for respect.

**Real toughness** is framed as a decision model under discomfort: experiencing discomfort/distress, “leaning in,” paying attention, and creating space for thoughtful action; maintaining a clear head for appropriate decisions. Magness states research shows this model works better than the old one.

Despite an easygoing “player’s coach” label, Carroll believes in toughness and is one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl.

He wants players who “come through when the game is on the line,” but defines toughness as inner drive to stay focused, embracing challenges and bouncing back, plus perseverance and passion. He “doesn’t shy away” from difficult practices via “always compete” drills, but he emphasizes that it’s his job to teach skills for handling adversity—“Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do and believing what they can do and they go out there and do it.”

Magness contrasts Carroll’s approach with the old model by mapping the shift: control → autonomy, appearance → substance, rigid push → flexibility, fear motivation → inner drive, insecurity → “quiet confidence.” He says the lesson generalizes: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy; in basketball John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni (“We keep it positive here”). Ken Reed is quoted: “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach. . . . Despite the success of Wooden, Shula, Dungy, Stevens, and others, our society has conditioned us to think that autocratic coaches are better coaches; that they win more often. It’s a myth. But it’s a vicious cycle.”

Magness adds science: a 2008 Eastern Washington study on nearly two hundred basketball players and their coaches concludes that mental-toughness “keys” don’t lie in “autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style,” but instead in the coach’s ability to create an environment emphasizing “trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

**Toughness maxim:** Real toughness is experiencing discomfort/distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action—“navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”

## “Searching for Real Toughness”: running as a laboratory of the mind
Magness shifts to autobiographical material about discovering what “tough” actually requires.

He recounts competing in the Don Bowden Mile: in 1957, Bowden was the first American to break the four-minute mile barrier; fifty years later, seven runners (six from UC Berkeley—plus Magness representing the University of Houston) chase the feat.

Racing strategy: get near the front early, “turn my brain off” by focusing on the runner ahead behind the “designated rabbits,” since “No one wins the race in the first half… they only lose it.” He zones out until the final lap where mental strength confronts pain/fatigue; first lap is 60 seconds; “Right on pace” is the only thought; midway includes coach calls “1:59 . . . 2:00.”

Magness explains fatigue as each runner’s “signature,” like rising shoulders, flailing arms, or contorted faces, and claims fatigue exposes breaking points. He says his weak point was always legs; breathing stayed “reliable—rhythmic and just on the right side of under control.”

Then at about 900 meters into the 1,609-meter race, he experiences early injury-like signs: neck tightening/straining, a strange breath, an almost high-pitched gasp “as if I’d swallowed some water and it went down the wrong tube.” His autopilot mind breaks into alarm: questions about too-soon failure and inability to breathe.

He tries familiar tough strategies—break race into pieces, ignore fatigue, push through—briefly succeeding. But under 100 meters later his inner voice screams “I can’t breathe… I can’t breathe!” He pulls off, halts, throws his head back, collapses onto knees, then the blockage sensation disappears after panic.

He searches for an explanation for a year: scopes down his throat, echocardiograms, treadmill/biking tests to exhaustion. Half a dozen specialists later, allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnoses paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD).

Magness explains VCD mechanics: vocal cords in the larynx open widely when breathing in, partially close when breathing out, and shut protectively to prevent objects passing into lower airways; opening/closing is mostly reflexive. In VCD, vocal cords “shut when they are supposed to open—essentially blocking the airways on inhalation.” The current theory: hyperresponsive vocal cords, “ready to shut at any moment,” like a “trigger-happy guard.” Severe cases cause inability-to-inhale sensation plus panic, fear, and anxiety; fear worsens symptoms.

He frames triggers: American Thoracic Society cites “strong emotions” and stress; other researchers point to hyperresponsive larynx and nervous system activity shifts that prime the body to close vocal cords as response to psychological or physical irritants. In his case, a normal “freak-out” moment while racing escalated into disaster.

He describes how his old “toughness” (pushing until he puked) backfired for the next year+ and notes he had to adopt a new tactic: relax, keep breathing/neck/mind steady at moments when discomfort and doubts are highest.

## The book’s scope and “toughness” claim
Magness says running will be a “central thread” because it is solitary “alone, in your head,” with immense discomfort. If readers aren’t endurance athletes, he says lessons apply beyond sport—to parenting, handling grief, and managing leading people “six or sixty years old.” Sources are described as experience with elite athletes and executives, plus “latest science” across cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and physiology.

He summarizes the core conclusion: “We have a fundamental misunderstanding of what toughness is.” Being tough isn’t a special reserved trait; it’s attainable if people adopt the correct framework. He says society overvalues facade perfectionism and “external signs” of strength; the book aims to emphasize real inner strength, compassion, grit, and grace—using Rich Roll’s quote: “Everybody goes through shit in their life. Nobody escapes obstacles.”

Real toughness is also framed as health-oriented (not only pain handling/performance): it involves preparing for, communicating with, responding to, and “transcend[ing] discomfort,” improving how to handle emotions/arguments and avoid burnout.

He previews four “pillars”:
1) Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
2) Listen to Your Body
3) Respond Instead of React
4) Transcend Discomfort

## Where the old model comes from: dependence on control
The chapter also points forward: why people keep adopting the Knight/authoritarian “facade of toughness” model. (The subsequent chapters then explain the pillars.)

---

## Later chapter excerpt (Chapter 10): building environments for internal toughness
The provided text includes substantial content labeled “Chapter 10,” which extends the toughness argument through leadership and motivational science.

### Cult/team dynamics vs controlling leaders
Magness uses a story about Julie, a college freshman, facing a coach who tells her competitors/enemies language, ranks players on an office door “from top to bottom” by favoritism, and uses stinging comments about her weight/personal life (including “Sex makes you gain weight”), plus “It’s us against the world.” Julie compares it to a cult.

Magness then specifies a cultlike environment and claims controlling leaders create dependency through four elements: controlling rewards, negative conditional regard, intimidation/isolation, and excessive personal control.

He argues “genius” explanations (e.g., Steve Jobs as “world-class jerk,” per Forbes phrasing) do not justify abusive styles when discussing old-school toughness.

### Inner drive vs external pressure
Magness challenges Protestant-work-ethic assumptions: people need external carrots/sticks, or they’ll stop working. He counters with a meta-analysis over 120 years and with Gallup data: “less than 2 percent overlap between salary and job satisfaction,” and “no relationship between employee engagement and level of pay” in a Gallup study of “over 1.4 million employees.” A “recent analysis” finds inner-drive motivation produces “three times more” engagement than external.

He ties toughness to persistence “directly” and says persistence also depends on “our why,” not only perceived control. He describes studies across domains (cycling, math, calling for donations) where persistence comes from alignment with identity/enjoyment/contentment, not fear/guilt/pressure or money.

A British athletes study of over one hundred athletes is cited as finding inner drive improves persistence on demanding exercise tests and toughness traits: seeing challenges as opportunities rather than threats and using positive coping instead of dissociative/disengagement strategies; internal motivation produces more positive emotions and higher willingness to repeat the task.

He contrasts with external-pressure motivation described as fragile: it leads to disengagement and giving up when despair hits; in his cited study, externally motivated individuals were more likely to disengage and see endeavors as threat.

### Persistence is not enough: reengage
Magness emphasizes “reengaging” as a toughness skill—shifting goals when demands make persistence irrational or dangerous. He gives an Everest analysis (nearly one hundred years): of climbers who reached the “death zone” above 8,000 meters, “only 10 percent died while making their way up,” while “73 percent perished on their way back down.” The implied choice is to abandon the goal to survive; toughness includes reframing and shifting targets (e.g., peak → safe descent).

He adds that researchers link reengaging not to control-based motivation but to within-driven autonomy: people with internal motivation adjust actions when goals become unattainable, switching to different attainable targets (example given: stuck writing a novel can shift from drafting a chapter to outlining thoughts).

He labels this motivational concept autonomous motivation and connects it to listening to the body to make the right decision under difficult moments.

### Self-determination theory (SDT): needs as fuel
Magness explains SDT through Deci/Ryan experiments with Tetris-like blocks: twenty-four students build shapes; when half receive monetary reward for each solved puzzle on day two, work increases; on day three when rewards are removed, motivation drops and participants spend less time and quit earlier.

He generalizes to the role of well-being and proposes three innate psychological needs for self-motivation and growth: autonomy, competence, relatedness.

He claims SDT applications span parenting, teaching, and substance abuse; needs satisfaction is linked to health, well-being ratings, and performance across domains, and helps persistence.

John Mahoney’s work is described as linking needs satisfaction to persistence; multiple studies tie it to willingness to put forth effort, improved concentration, challenge seeking, and better stress coping. He notes autonomy/support increases self-esteem and emotional intelligence.

A study with over two hundred cross-country runners and rowers reports satisfying needs correlates with toughness and improved racing times; Mahoney finds social environment (mainly coach) affects whether athletes meet needs. In supportive atmospheres fostering autonomy and belonging, athletes show greater toughness and performance, concluding toughness results from “coaching behaviors that promote psychological needs satisfaction.”

**Toughness maxim (repeated):** When we satisfy our needs, we are allowed to fulfill our potential; needs satisfaction “is the fuel” to apply toughness tools.

### Coaching/leadership implications and evidence
Magness contrasts old-school demands/authority with SDT: authoritarian control, fear/punishment, and control-based obedience do not create intrinsic motivation; instead they create its opposite.

He cites organizational psychologist Erica Carleton and sports psychologist Mark Beauchamp studying fifty-seven NBA head coaches (2000–2006). Using newspaper/magazine/interview evidence, trained psychologists assess “abusive leadership” (ridicule/blame to motivate/teach, e.g., telling players they aren’t competent/tough enough). Across nearly seven hundred players’ performance (player efficiency score), abusive leadership yields clear performance drops and career-long effects: the career trajectory shifts downward and players later have more technical fouls (aggression indicator).

He frames the leader’s role: dictating autonomy and shaping belonging/progress risk. He asks if leaders create cult-style dependency, whether people can take risks, if support exists, whether teammates are framed as threats. Control-based environments increase pressure/fear, aggression, burnout, and reduce performance/well-being; needs-satisfying leadership yields tougher, healthier humans.

A report from sports psychologist Laura Healy is included: autonomy-supportive coaches correspond to athletes reporting higher basic-need satisfaction and higher autonomous motives.

### Chapter 10’s three “need” supports
Magness then turns SDT into a leadership toolkit:

1) **Support, not thwart:** autonomy supportive leadership as guidance “on the journey” and choices/ownership. He gives a Golden State Warriors example: Steve Kerr hands over coaching to players (Feb 2018), turning over coaching duties before win #44; for a game vs Phoenix Suns, Kerr lets Iguodala/Green draw plays; Warriors win 129–83, and Kerr says it was because “It’s the players’ team… they have to take ownership of it… I don’t feel like we focused well at all the last month.”

He cites Eastern Washington comparison: servant/supportive vs power/thwarting styles across sixty-four NCAA track teams; servant-led athletes score higher on mental toughness and run faster.

He gives workplace evidence: in a study of over one thousand office workers, the strongest predictor for coping with demanding work was whether they felt respected/valued by managers.

2) **Can I make progress?** Competence as visibility of progress and mastery pathways. He emphasizes that without a plausible route to growth, motivation collapses (no easy rationalization because objective metrics drive self-belief losses). He stresses the role of “psychological safety,” defined as voice/risk-taking without fear of punishment (not “safe spaces”). He notes Google’s two-year team study and its top characteristic: “Can we take risks on this team without feeling insecure or embarrassed?”

3) **A need to belong:** connection/trust and cooperation. He cites Michael Kraus, Cassey Huang, and Dacher Keltner’s 2010 paper: coding nearly three hundred NBA player behaviors in 2008–2009; not points, assists, blocks, rebounds, but cooperation/trust signals (fist bumps, high fives, short conversations, setting screens). Teams with those behaviors had better performance. Magness clarifies the takeaway: acts are not the goal; the representation of belonging/trust is.

He cites Scott Barry Kaufman on belonging: acceptance/being seen vs rejection/invisibility. He claims rejection activates pain-like responses in the brain.

He introduces neurobiology: calm-and-connect system vs fight-or-flight. Feel-good opioids dampen cortisol; oxytocin turns down threat response (amygdala) and increases cooperation, but only when the other is deemed trustworthy. He notes “social recovery” strategies in professional sports (postgame social interaction) as a way to transition from stressed to recover-and-adapt states.

He uses Gregg Popovich/Spurs team meals as an example: meticulous, long meals with wine/food, arranging tables to maximize interaction, staying after games rather than immediately leaving. He also cites a 2003 study on soldiers fighting in Iraq War: bonds of trust/friendship/group identity were built most during “noncombat time”—“hours of nothingness, the shared boredom,” emphasizing conversation during it.

He argues forced bonding fails: other professional teams copied postgame meals but reported “We hosted team dinners, and no one showed up” and “No one talked,” so the lesson is creating a space for bonding rather than the activity itself. He argues cohesion requires real invitations—authenticity, not gimmicks.

### Maslow hierarchy and self-transcendence
Magness ends this excerpt by linking SDT to Maslow. He notes Maslow’s hierarchy includes both physiological needs (food, water, sleep) and psychological needs (safety, belonging, self-esteem). He corrects a common misreading: the “famous pyramid” featuring self-actualization wasn’t Maslow’s intended form; in 1970 Maslow wrote, “I realized I’d rather leave [self-actualization] behind me. Just too sloppy & too easily criticizable.” Magness says Maslow’s highest rung in final rendering is “self-transcendence,” rising above individual concerns.

He argues that society’s “mask of toughness” hides idealism and transcendent experiences; satisfying basic psychological needs lets people reach potential, handle fear/pressure, and grow as humans—via belonging/acceptance rather than control.

## Chapter 11 excerpt (Find Meaning in Discomfort): purpose, suffering, and exploration
The provided text also includes Chapter 11 content, focusing on meaning.

### Meaning’s role in fulfillment and suffering
Magness describes a lecture series attended by a professor (MD pursuing a PhD) with course topics (“Suicide-forced annihilation, the world of the mentally ill, sexual education”) and a final lecture called “Experimentum Crucis.” The professor argues joy cannot be pursued as a goal; happiness “should not, must not, and can never be a goal, but only an outcome.” Fulfillment comes from three keys: doing (creating/labor of love), experiencing (nature/love/art/awe), and—surprisingly for the audience—suffering.

He quotes the professor: “True suffering of an authentic fate is an achievement, and, indeed, is the highest possible achievement.” Meaning is extracted from suffering: suffering “strips us of our vanities” and allows determination of one’s reaction. The doctor’s claim is that meaning is determined “by ‘the individual, and only that individual,’” and Frankl is used as a model (he later delivered a similar lecture at “The Psychology of the Concentration Camp”).

### Viktor Frankl: phases, will to survive, and meaning as freedom
Magness narrates Frankl’s concentration camp experience (Theresienstadt), including that Frankl entered in 1942 with a manuscript sewn into his jacket pocket that was confiscated. He reports the psychological phases: shock and momentary suicide escape fantasies at first; then apathy/normalization where inner life reduced to a minimum, emotions subside to a “Hmm,” and thoughts narrow to food. He cites survivors Lou and Esther reporting “numb and living a day at a time… Your brains don’t work. First, you want to die. Then you want to survive.”

Frankl’s argument is that one part remains free: “their own minds,” and that seeing meaning in every moment is the key to will to survive or to peace in death. Magness quotes Frankl on “freedom” and on dying “a death of our own and not the death that the SS had forced on us.”

Frankl’s personal meaning is described as reconstructing his lost manuscript; writing gave meaning, and a pencil/scraps in 1945 provided boost. Magness quotes Frankl’s conclusion about “unconditional meaning” making life bearable and notes research confirms similar themes in survivors.

### Purpose as a toughness fuel (drive under fatigue)
Magness also provides a “will to continue” model: in an exercise science framing, he presents performance = Actual effort / Expected Effort * Drive. He argues drive/motivation/purpose determines how close to fatigue “zero” one can push. He analogizes the body to a car with a mileage countdown showing “leeway” between the display of empty and actual empty; the body uses a safety mechanism/alarm that slows before catastrophic failure, and perceived risk/reward and task importance determine how close to zero the “governor” is set.

He claims purpose acts like a “turbo boost” and links purpose with persistence in classroom, workplace, and athletic fields.

**Toughness maxim:** Purpose is the fuel that allows you to be tough.

### Avoidance vs exploration; post-traumatic growth
Magness explains meaning’s continued role beyond Holocaust survivors: it applies to trauma and post-traumatic growth (PTG). He argues PTG is not limited to milder trauma; for Vietnam War POWs, “the longer a POW spent in captivity, the more physical injuries,” and growth was higher. Severe trauma shatters worldview assumptions, prompting meaning-search and reconstruction of inner narrative.

He notes that PTG doesn’t mean avoidance; people experience similar rumination but shift it from intrusive to deliberate and constructive rumination (deliberate rumination focuses on problem-solving; self-talk is reflective/nonjudgmental). He says shifting requires sense of control and emotion regulation, and cites Todd Kashdan’s study of over 170 college students on grief/accidents/violence: the highest growth came from those who navigated anxiety/trauma through exploration rather than avoidance.

Meaning is framed as “glue” holding mind together so it stalls the jump from difficulty to despair and from fear/anxiety to freak-out; he includes Frankl’s line about freedom to adapt “in one way or another—and indeed there was a ‘one way or another.’”

## System meaning + “evolving best structure”
External organization must be “better than your mental one” so you can let go of lower-level thinking and keep focus on the broader horizon. “Being organized” means where something lives (physical/digital) matches what it means to you (reference goes to reference; a call reminder goes where calls reminders live). This hinges on clarifying **What does something mean to you?** Core distinctions hold, but the “best structure” can evolve as you process and test your system.

## Seven buckets (hard edges)
Seven primary categories to keep track of:
- Projects list
- Project support material
- Calendar actions and information
- Next Actions lists
- A Waiting For list
- Reference material
- A Someday/Maybe list

Categories must be **pristinely distinct** (visually, physically, and psychologically) because each is a discrete self-agreement about *when and how* you’ll be reminded; blending edges causes “psychological numbness” and broken trust: reference mixed with things you still want to read; day-specific items mistakenly placed on Next Actions (undermining calendar trust and forcing reassessment); projects you won’t act on for some time moved off Projects to Someday/Maybe; Waiting For items placed on action lists leading to nonproductive rethinking.

## Lists + folders (no scaffolding)
After contents are clarified, you “all you really need are lists and folders” for reminders, reference, and support materials. Lists hold projects/someday/maybes and active open-loop **actions**; folders hold **reference** and project support for active projects. A “list” can be: (1) a container/folder of separate paper notes, (2) a titled list page, or (3) an inventory in software/digital devices. Avoid creating priority “scaffolding” you’ll later rewrite; the list is the master inventory for review and intuitive prioritization.

## Organizing action reminders
Pending reminders after in-tray processing are longer-than-two-minute personal actions that can’t be delegated, reminders of delegated items, and items needing calendar placement or Someday/Maybe storage; sort/group for review based on how you work.

### Calendar: only hard edges
Two action types: (1) must be done on a certain **day and/or time** (time-specific or day-specific); (2) “as soon as possible” around calendar constraints (possibly with a final due date). The calendar should show only the “hard landscape” (exact day commitments visible at a glance); resist writing actions as “next Monday” if they might shift.

### Next Actions: as-soon-as-possible by required context
“As soon as I can” actions should be reminded by the **context required** (tool/location/situation). Context categories depend on (1) how many next actions you track and (2) how often contexts change; too many on one list causes repeated re-sorting and window-hunting. Energy lever: switching tools/modes costs more energy than most people realize. 

Common Next Actions headings include: **Calls** (record phone number alongside each item), **At Computer**, **Online** (example: maintained separately so offline flights don’t break At Computer assumptions), **Errands**, **At Office** (miscellaneous; sometimes At Office A/B for “hotel-ing”), **At Home**, **Anywhere**, **Agendas** (items to cover in real-time interactions/meetings; separate Agenda lists for standing meetings/people; recommended range **three to fifteen**; separate lists for bosses/partners/assistants/children; also for attorney/financial adviser/accountant/computer consultant, plus ad hoc limited-duration interaction lists like a contractor on site), and **Read/Review** (printed reading longer than two minutes; optionally **Review/Respond** and/or a digital parallel like “Review/Watch”).

### Waiting For: responsibility without next-action confusion
Waiting For tracks final deliverables/projects whose next steps depend on others. Keep it close at hand with Next Actions reminders; review as often as needed to decide whether to trigger follow-up. Operational rules: keep current/complete/reviewed; update responsibility as next steps change (e.g., request proposal → Waiting For; proposal review → Read/Review or At Computer; send to boss for approval → back to Waiting For); include **requested-for date** and **agreed-upon due date** for grounded follow-up.

### Originating documents as their own reminders (with edges preserved)
Often add reminders to lists/folders when captured, letting the originating trigger vanish. Some inputs can serve as their own reminders if logistics make sense: paper reading to labeled Read/Review trays/stacks; bills to Bills to Pay / Financial to Process stacks; receipts to Receipts to Process envelope/folder; work logistics may require reminders only at the workstation. Reminders must stay in discrete categories based on the **next action required**; mixing different-action items of the same document type in one tray/file leads to mind numbness.

### E-mail workflow: empty in-tray via @ACTION / @WAITING FOR
Actionable e-mails can be stored as reminders inside e-mail with folder prefixes:
- **@ACTION**: longer-than-two-minute action e-mails
- **@WAITING FOR**: delegated responsibility (move relevant e-mails; include cc:/bcc: copies when delegating)

“Getting e-mail ‘in’ to empty” means: delete, file reference, complete less-than-two-minute responses, and move Waiting For + actionable e-mails into reminder folders—*not* “everything is done.”

### Caution: don’t disperse action triggers out of sight
If triggers are offscreen/out of sight, the system stops performing its core function (visible reminders you can trust). Before leaving office/shifting modes, pending actionable e-mails must be individually reviewed; **@ACTION behaves like an extension of At Computer**. Offscreen digital reminders can disappear; some revert to paper planners for trust. You must be able to know within seconds what actionable items exist and that they will wait.

## Organizing project reminders
A **project** is a commitment/outcome requiring more than one action step. Projects list is an **index of open loops**, not where you do the work moment-to-moment; day-to-day execution comes from calendar, action lists, and unexpected tasks. Value comes from **weekly review (at least once a week)**: verify action steps exist for all projects, nothing slips, and inventory supports workload evaluation.

### What counts as a project + where “look into” fits
Definition is broad: more than one action needed to achieve a desired result, including “look into” efforts even if not project-like. Reasons to keep projects complete/current: unreviewed projects occupy mind space; projects can morph from small to larger issues; Weekly Review needs the projects index; relationship management relies on overview of explicit/implicit agreements.

### Hidden projects: three sources
1) current activities (meetings/calls/trips with unresolved outcomes; proposals/contracts/forms as project artifacts/components)
2) higher-horizon interests/commitments (roles/accountabilities, professional goals/company objectives/strategic plans, personal items like kids/parents aging, retirement, life partner aspirations, fun/creative things)
3) current problems/issues/opportunities (problems are always projects—solution may be unclear—plus admin/workflow frustrations like filing/storage/communication/hiring/tracking/record keeping, expense reporting, banking/investing, staying in touch). Learning/experience desires may be Someday/Maybe or Projects depending on desired outcomes.

### One Projects list vs subdividing
Most people do best with one master Projects list if it’s complete/current and reviewed sufficiently (often in Weekly Review). Subdivision can help reduce anxiety or separate life domains (personal vs professional; delegated projects; specific types like “Projects—Presentations”; sales relationships in progress; areas of focus/roles), but structure should change as experience shifts (“optimal simplicity”).

### Subprojects + dependencies
Format isn’t perfect: if you make a large project one Projects-list entry (e.g., “Finish new home upgrades”), you can keep components/subprojects as **project support material** reviewed with that major item. If dependencies block progress, subcomponents may appear without next actions; independent components keep next actions current. If unsure, Allen’s fallback: keep big projects on Projects list and store subpieces in project support for Weekly Review, or list active independent subprojects separately.

### Project support material: resources, not reminder triggers
Project support material supports actions/thinking; it is not where primary reminders should live. Don’t use support stacks/files/e-mails as primary reminders because next actions/Waiting For remain psychologically embedded, producing a subliminal chant (“Do something about me! Decide something about me! Follow up with something about me!”). Correct sequence: (1) add project to Projects list, (2) create next actions/Waiting For in the appropriate lists, (3) pull support materials for execution or during Weekly Review.

## Organizing nonactionable data
Systems fail when actionable items mix with nonactionable data. Nonactionable items fall into: **reference materials**, **reminders for later reassessment**, and **trash**.

### Reference material: a library with no pull
Reference requires no action and should have no incompletion/pull after you distinguish actionable vs nonactionable. You decide what to keep, how much, and where; increasing pure reference can add little psychological weight. Reference system options include: general-reference filing (1–4 physical drawers, many dozens e-mail folders, a few to hundreds digital categories); large-category filing for topics needing >50 folders/major documents; contact managers as reference data (not action reminders unless CRM integrates action triggers); libraries/archives at personalized levels. No perfect system: start from what you truly want to keep, make it retrievable, and course-correct via regular overview.

### Someday/Maybes: managed back-burner commitments
Someday/Maybes are on-hold items for reassessment later (trip ideas, books to read, future fiscal year projects, skills to learn). Not throwaway items; may be most creative commitments. Recommended: a Someday/Maybe list for items you’re not sure you want to commit to yet, with examples: “Learn Spanish,” “Get Marcie a horse,” “Climb Mt. Washington,” “Write a mystery novel,” “Get a vacation cottage.” Optional: subcategorize (e.g., “parking-lot ideas” vs bucket-list fantasies like climbing a mountain in Nepal or creating a foundation for disadvantaged kids). Avoid “Hold and Review” piles/files because often they’re held but not reviewed, creating numbness/resistance and disappearing value. A catchall bucket mixing destinations/reminder types is risky; Someday/Maybe must be consciously revisited.

### Calendar for future options + tickler file
Calendar can park triggers for later reassessment (activate projects, events to decide about, decision catalysts) including “decide-not-to-decide.” Decision catalysts cover significant delayed decisions due to internal timing (sleep on it) or strategic timing (last responsible moment). Typical decision areas listed: hire/fire; merge/acquire/sell/divest; change job/career; potential strategy redirection.

A **tickler file** is a low-tech 3D calendar that brings physical reminders into your in-tray on future dates (“mail” to yourself). Allen’s physical setup requires **forty-three folders**: **thirty-one** labeled “1”–“31” plus **twelve** month folders; daily files sit in front starting with tomorrow, emptied into in-tray daily and refilled for perpetual movement; monthlies similarly refill for the next year’s months. It demands daily check/update (one-second-per-day) or you won’t trust it; if you miss the weekend or leave town, check folders for days you’ll be away.

## Checklists as external mind
Checklists are external “recipes of potential ingredients” for review structure across projects/work/processes/events/areas of value. Purpose: entrust details to external mind (Whitehead: “Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.”). 

For fuzzier internal commitments, translate to inherent projects/actions when possible (e.g., “Exercise more regularly” → “Set up regular exercise program” + action like calling Sally for gym/trainer suggestions; “Maintain good morale on my team” → project exploring team-building processes + action to e-mail HR director). For responsibilities needing overview, build blueprint checklists reviewed regularly across layers/outcomes/standards, including: Career goals; Service; Family; Relationships; Community; Health and energy; Financial resources; Creative expression, plus job-level accountability items (team morale, processes, timelines, staff issues, workload, communications, technology). Need for checklists depends on unfamiliarity; novelty/temporary role shocks require more external control until “cruise control” returns.

Create/eliminate checklists as needed and store them where easily accessible (loose-leaf notebook or readily available software). Appropriately used, checklists relieve mental pressure.

- **Projects list**
- **Project support material**
- **Calendar actions and information**
- **Next Actions lists**
- **A Waiting For list**
- **Reference material**
- **A Someday/Maybe list**

All categories must stay **pristinely distinct** (visually, physically, and psychologically). Each represents a discrete self-agreement about *when and in what way* you will be reminded. If edges blur, value is lost: you become psychologically numb when different meanings share the same pile. Examples of failure modes:
- Mixing reference with items you still plan to read makes you go unconscious to the stack.
- Putting time-specific actions on Next Actions lists breaks calendar trust and forces ongoing reassessment.

- **Lists** track projects/someday/maybes and actions for open loops.
- **Folders (digital/paper)** hold reference and support information for active projects.

Simplicity caveat: don’t create extra external “priority scaffolding” that you’ll later rearrange/rewrite; the system supports intuitive prioritizing by keeping the list as a master inventory for review.

A “list” can be: (1) a folder/container with separate notes, (2) a titled list page in a planner/loose-leaf, or (3) an inventory on a software/digital device.

Once your in-tray is empty, you have:
- “Pending reminders” for longer-than-two-minute actions that cannot be delegated, and
- reminders for delegated things, plus
- items needing calendar placement or Someday/Maybe storage.

You sort/group these for review as work options and place them physically/digitally in folders/lists.

### Actions that go on your calendar (“hard landscape”)
Two kinds of actions exist: 
1) actions that must occur on a certain **day and/or time**, and
2) actions that need doing **as soon as possible** around calendar constraints (possibly with a due date).

The calendar should show only the **hard landscape**—exact commitments visible at a glance while you’re “on the run.” Avoid old habit: don’t pre-place actions on future days you’d “like” to do but may not; only calendar what’s truly day/time-specific so the rest remain in “as soon as possible” handling.

### Organizing as-soon-as-possible actions by context
The best way to remind yourself of “as soon as I can” is **context**, defined by the **tool/location/situation** needed to complete the action.
- Computer-dependent → **At Computer** list
- Out-and-about errands → **Errands** list
- Face-to-face with a person → e.g., **Emily** folder/list

How many context categories to use depends on (1) how many next actions you track and (2) how often context changes. With many actions, a single list becomes unproductive sorting; with fewer actions (e.g., rare “twenty-five” next actions), a single Next Actions list could suffice.

Context categories also support energy management: “phone mode” → Calls list, “computer mode” → At Computer, plus the note that switching between behavior/tool modes takes more energy than most people realize.

#### Most common next-action categories (examples and rules)
Common headings include:
- **Calls**
- **At Computer**
- **Errands**
- **At Office (miscellaneous)**
- **At Home**
- **Anywhere**
- **Agendas (for people and meetings)**
- **Read/Review**

Key details inside categories:
- **Calls**: record the phone number alongside each item; a phone-available context enables focus.
- **At Computer**: helpful when multiple computers (work/home/laptop/tablet) exist. Allen separates “Online” from At Computer because flying without Wi‑Fi means At Computer actions shouldn’t require web/server connectivity.
- **Errands**: useful to group multiple tasks in one trip; example errands given: “Get stock certificates from bank deposit box,” “Pick up suit at the tailor,” “Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist.”
  - Sub-lists can be created (e.g., a “hardware store” item with appended sub-items).
  - A caution on GPS/location-based reminders: sensible in principle, but with variables and the need for integrated overview and review, they’re “only…a nice option to add” rather than trusted to keep your head clear.
- **At Office**: for actions requiring physical presence; with “hotel-ing,” “At Office” may mean any company location, or separate “At Office A/B” lists may apply.
- **At Home**: for actions doable only at home; example items: “Hang new watercolor print,” “Organize travel accessories,” “Switch closets to winter clothes.”

#### Agendas
Many next actions need real-time interaction in conversation/committee/meeting; Allen’s term **Agenda** corresponds to items to cover with someone or in a meeting (not “calendar/schedule/diary” in other cultures).
- Keep separate Agenda lists for standing meetings and for people you deal with ongoing.
- Number of Agenda lists can range from **three to fifteen**, with recommended separation for roles like bosses, partners, assistants, children.
- Also keep Agenda lists for roles like attorney, financial adviser, accountant, computer consultant, etc.
- For temporary/limited interactions (e.g., a contractor on site), maintain a list for that person for the duration.

#### Read/Review
Items whose next action is **reading** should be handled after applying the two-minute rule: quick-skims dispatched; longer-than-two-minute printed items go in a labeled tray/stack called **Read/Review**.
- The category needs “pristine delineation” to prevent it becoming psychologically numbing.
- For professionals with much printed material (e.g., attorneys), there may also be a stricter **Review/Respond** category.
- Read/Review organization is practical for “weird little windows” (waiting, trains/planes, seminars).
- For digital input, a parallel bucket can exist (e.g., “Review/Watch” in e-mail or a Surf Web action list) for noncritical but interesting data.

### Organizing “Waiting For”
Waiting For tracks final deliverables/projects where next steps are up to others, not discrete personal action steps. Examples: theater tickets ordered, a scanner arriving for the office, client OK on a proposal.

This list is reviewed as needed to decide whether you should trigger an action (e.g., check status, apply pressure) to move deliverables.

Operational/relationship logic:
- Keeping the Waiting For inventory captured/current/complete/reviewed improves relief and focus.
- It’s best kept close at hand in the same system as Next Actions lists.
- Items may move back and forth between categories as responsibility and next steps change (e.g., request proposal → Waiting For; proposal review → Read/Review tray or At Computer; send to boss for approval → back to Waiting For).
- Digital list managers/low-tech folders have an advantage moving items across categories without rewriting.

Follow-up effectiveness depends on including a **requested-for date** and **agreed-upon due date**; Allen emphasizes the tactical value of being able to say things like “But I placed the order March twentieth” or “You’ve had the proposal now for three weeks.”

### Using the original item as its own reminder
Efficiency rule: the best tracking method is adding action reminders to lists/folders as they occur; the originating trigger doesn’t need to remain once processed.

Exceptions: some inputs are their own reminders.

#### Managing paper-based workflow
- Putting reminders for items you’ll read directly into the **Read/Review** tray avoids writing “Review Vogue magazine” elsewhere.
- For paper bills: instead of writing a list item, use a folder/stack tray labeled “Bills to Pay” (or “Financial to Process”) to batch bill-paying.
- Receipts for expense reporting: deal with them at generation or store in “Receipts to Process” envelope/folder.

Caution: danger arises if you don’t put these physical piles in front of your face and review consistently; “organized” isn’t sufficient—trust requires consistent review.

Logistics rule: decide based on whether you can do the work away from your desk; if you can’t, reminders should be managed only at your workstation.

#### Reducing cognitive load via discrete next-action categories
Core reason for organizing is to reduce cognitive load: prevent constant mental questioning (“what do I need to do about this?”).

A critical warning: keeping documents of one type in a single tray/file even when their **next actions differ** causes mind numbness because decision-making is deferred to later (phone call vs. data review vs. waiting for someone).

Allen’s personal note: his system is portable with lists, but he still maintains a **Read/Review stack tray** and a traveling **plastic folder** titled the same way.

#### Managing e-mail-based workflow
Some actionable e-mails are best stored as reminders *within the e-mail system itself*—especially when e-mail software is always active.

Allen’s recommended folder approach:
- Create **@ACTION** folder for longer-than-two-minute action e-mails; prefix letter/symbol so it sorts to top.
- Create **@WAITING FOR** folder; move relevant e-mails there when someone else is responsible (including cc:/bcc: copies when delegating).
- If some e-mail apps support “Send and File,” it can vary; otherwise, cc/bcc to self and place into @WAITING FOR.

Follow-through claim: it takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand.

### Getting e-mail “in” to empty
“Getting ‘in’ empty” means not that everything is done, but that the e-mail “in-tray” is cleared of staging/actionable items: delete, file reference, complete less-than-two-minute responses, and move waiting-for and actionable e-mails into reminder folders.

If your in area contains staging/ref/trashed items, you must reassess everything every time you glance, rapidly numbing the mind.

In the resulting system, you open **@ACTION** and review only e-mails you’ve decided to spend time on, instead of fearing missing something across multiple screens.

### Caution about dispersing action reminders
Danger: action triggers stored out of sight fail to provide reminders when needed. Organization’s function is supplying reminders you must see when you need them.

Before leaving the office or shifting into planned/unplanned work, you must review all actionable e-mails individually just like Calls and At Computer lists. @ACTION behaves like an extension of At Computer.

Paper-based pending workflow likewise must be reviewed like a list if papers are your only reminders.

Digital risk: offscreen data can disappear as a viable prompt; some computer-savvy people revert to paper for trust.

Bottom-line requirement: you must know within seconds where actionable items are and that they will wait; not days.

## Organizing project reminders
Projects list experience: creating a comprehensive list of commitments/outcomes requiring more than one action step yields major control. Initially you can make a master list or separate sheets/folders labeled “Projects.”

### Projects list(s)
Projects list is an **index of open loops**, not a plan/details store, and not arranged by priority/size/urgency. Moment-to-moment work comes from calendar, action lists, and unexpected tasks; projects provide the horizon for comfort and planning.

Primary value comes from **complete review at least once a week** to ensure:
- action steps exist for all projects,
- nothing slips through cracks,
- inventory supports workload evaluation and control glance.

Allen frames it as: complete and current Projects list is the operational tool for moving from “tree-hugging” to “forest management.”

#### Why a complete Projects list matters (reasons)
Broad definition: “more than one action needed to achieve a desired result.” This net captures subtle pressures even if the domain calls them something else (Allen explicitly lists “look into getting a dog for our kids” and “find a good tailor” as projects).

Reasons listed:
- **Critical for control and focus** (unreviewed projects keep pulling at mind; “I’ve got to get my driver’s license renewed” can occupy as much space as “I need to formulate the agenda for next year’s conference”).
- **Alleviates subtle tensions** (projects often start small and morph; examples include preschool registration forms/logistics, invoice dispute turning into larger issue).
- **Core of the Weekly Review** (projects list must already exist to orient weekly review).
- **Facilitates relationship management** (having overview of commitments enables negotiations about explicit/implicit agreements).

#### Where to look for hidden projects
Three primary sources:
1) **Current activities**: scheduled meetings/calls/trips that represent incomplete outcomes; example: a scheduled conference call is actually about “Look into possible custom program for Client XYZ.” Also includes proposals/contracts/forms/broken-watch artifacts that are project components.
2) **Higher-horizon interests and commitments**: role/accountabilities, professional goals/company objectives/strategic plans, personal life items (kids/parents aging, retirement, life partner aspirations, fun/creative things).
3) **Current problems, issues, and opportunities**: problems are always projects (even if resolution unknown, there is research to do). Examples provided: “Look into improving Frederick ’s relationship with his school,” “Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance,” “Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner.” Also includes workflow/admin frustrations (filing/storage/communication/hiring/tracking/record keeping, expense reporting, banking/investing, staying in touch).

A final category inside opportunities: learning/experience desires (e.g., “learn Italian cooking,” “how to draw,” “take an online course in digital photography or social media marketing”) that may live on Someday/Maybe unless you decide to define desired outcomes on Projects.

### One list or subdivided?
Most people do best with **one Projects list** as master inventory rather than daily prioritizing guideline; you can look across multiple lists in Weekly Review. How many lists is “not nearly as critical as ensuring that your inventory is complete, current, and assessed sufficiently.”

Allen describes several reasons people subdivide:
- **Personal/Professional**: personal list reviewed as judiciously as professional; personal pressures can create greatest professional stress.
- **Delegated Projects**: senior managers may separate into “Projects—Delegated” while ensuring they move via regular review.
- **Specific types of projects**: e.g., “Projects—Presentations” as chronological upcoming events for a corporate trainer/keynote speaker.
- **Sales relationships in progress**: can maintain a separate view for outstanding sales relationships, reviewed for current actions.
- **Areas of focus**: grouping by major focus areas/roles.

Allen caveat: if you change structure as experience shifts, it’s expected; “optimal simplicity” comes from whatever complexity yields optimal simplicity.

### What about subprojects?
Allen states the decision isn’t about format perfection: decide whether a large initiative like “Finish new home upgrades” is one Projects list entry with subpieces held as project support material, or whether each independent portion becomes a separate entry. The requirement is frequent review of all components.

If subprojects can’t proceed until others do, they may appear without next actions until dependencies clear (example: “Upgrade the kitchen” may depend on “Assess and upgrade home electrical system”). If independent, next actions should stay current on the independent component.

Allen’s advice (fallback): vote for putting big projects on Projects list and holding subpieces in project support material, reviewed via Weekly Review; but if it doesn’t feel right, include active independent subprojects separately.

### Project support materials
Support materials are neither project actions nor reminders. They are resources for supporting actions and thinking.

Core warning: don’t use support materials as primary reminders because you haven’t determined next actions/Waiting For items, so psychological pressure turns archives into “stuff” and creates subliminal demands: “Do something about me! Decide something about me! Follow up with something about me!”

Correct sequence:
1) add the project to Projects list,
2) put action steps onto action reminder lists and Waiting For items onto Waiting For,
3) pull support materials only when you need them for executing actions or doing Weekly Review.

Example: moving to a new residence—folder “Upgrades—37 Pinkerton Place” holds plans/details; during Weekly Review, when “Upgrade new residence” appears on Projects, you open the folder, identify any next actions from notes, then refile.

Client-folder/CRM caution: client information can be reference data in client reference files, but calls/reminders must live on action lists (e.g., “if I need to call a client, I don’t want that reminder embedded anywhere but on a Calls list”). Advanced CRM automation doesn’t eliminate the need for personal engagement/trust in practice.

### Organizing ad hoc project thinking
Ideas related to a project but not yet next actions belong as project support materials. Capture/attach and store where you’ll review.

Methods:
- **Attached notes**: attach notes to list/calendar entry in software; for paper Projects list, attach a Post-it or separate sheet next to the project item.
- **E-mail/software apps**: use dedicated e-mail reference folder for project-related information; possibly split into “Johnson Partnership—Active” and “Johnson Partnership—Archive.” Digital tools are abundant, but there’s risk of scattering information across too many locations without coordination/links.
- **Paper-based files**: separate folder per project; printing relevant items for planning sessions.
- **Pages in notebooks**: devote pages to project support.

Operational rule: consistently look for action steps inherent in project notes; review notes as often as needed; clear notes once stale to avoid “stale virus.”

## Organizing nonactionable data
Most systems fail because they blend actionable items with nonactionable data (clogging the process). Nonactionable items fall into three categories:
- reference materials,
- reminders for later reassessment,
- trash.

### Reference materials
Reference requires no action; it’s information you want to keep for future retrieval. Your attention on reference should only appear when changing the system because you have too much/too little.

Psychological requirement: decide what is actionable vs. nonactionable. After that, reference should have no incompletion/pull. The only remaining decision is how large a reference library you want.

Allen’s stance: you can keep lots of pure reference without psychological weight, especially as disk/storage expands.

#### Variety of reference systems
Allen surveys:
- **General-reference filing**: ideally set up during “in” processing; informal/accessibility matters; practical scale described as “one to four physical file drawers, many dozens of e-mail reference folders,” plus other digital storage locations that can range from a few to hundreds.
  - Example of growth: tracking restaurants globally in software can create “hundreds” of folders/subfolders like “Locales—London—Restaurants.”
- **Large-category filing**: topics requiring “more than fifty folders and/or major documents” get their own section/drawer/database with searchable organization. Example: corporate merger due diligence might require “two or three whole file cabinets”; hobbies like gardening/sailing/cooking might each get at least one file drawer.
- **Contact managers**: contact info (phone numbers, emails, etc.) is reference data; it should not be used for action reminders unless integrated CRM includes both data and action triggers.
  - Caveat: digital contact manager adoption can still leave business-card piles “subtly yelling at them, ‘Decide something about me! Do something with me!’”
- **Libraries/archives at personalized levels**: storage is logistical/purpose-based. Determine ubiquity (mobile device for always-needed, briefcase for meetings/off-site, office filing for onsite, cloud/archived for rare situations). If you need something offline, print it when online.

No perfect reference system; start from real information you want to keep, place it where it’s retrievable, and course-correct through regular overview.

### Someday/Maybes
Someday/Maybes are “back burner/on hold” items for reassessment later: special trip ideas, books to read, projects for a future fiscal year, skills to learn.

Someday/Maybes are explicitly not throwaway items; they can be the most interesting/creative commitments.

#### Someday/Maybe list and sources
Allen recommends a Someday/Maybe list for everything you’re not sure you want to commit to yet. Examples given: “Learn Spanish,” “Get Marcie a horse,” “Climb Mt. Washington,” “Write a mystery novel,” “Get a vacation cottage.”

Two rich sources to populate it:
- creative imagination,
- review of current projects.

Allen also notes some things may happen “almost without your making any conscious effort” when you have permission to imagine.

He lists typical Someday/Maybe inventory categories: 
- Things to get/build for home; hobbies; skills; creative expressions; clothes/accessories; toys; trips; organizations to join; service projects; things to see/do.

Reassess current Projects: if optional projects have no chance of attention for “the next few months or more,” move them to Someday/Maybe.

Subcategorizing is allowed to separate “parking lot” ideas vs. bucket-list fantasies like climbing a mountain in Nepal or creating a foundation for disadvantaged kids (the distinction is described without requiring a specific implementation).

#### Special categories and cross-role lists
Allen provides examples of special Someday/Maybe categories that can be partly reference/partly Someday/Maybe:
- Food (recipes, menus, restaurants, wines), Children, Books, Music, Movies, Gift ideas, Web sites, Weekend trips, Ideas—Misc.

### Danger of “Hold and Review” files/piles
Allen does not recommend “Hold and Review” drawers/piles because in most cases people held but didn’t review; it creates numbness/resistance and the value disappears without consistent awareness.

A key differentiation: Someday/Maybe is managed; a catchall bucket usually contains a mix that should be tossed, moved to Read/Review, filed as reference, put on calendar or tickler, assigned next actions, etc.

Allen concludes that after processing someone’s “Hold and Review” drawer/file, he often finds “there was nothing left in it!”

### Using the calendar for future options
Calendar can store day-specific triggers for later reassessment, including:
- triggers to activate projects,
- events to decide about,
- decision catalysts.

Examples of project activation triggers include lead-time tasks (product launches, fund-raisers), regular preparation (budget reviews, annual conferences, planning events), and key dates for significant people (birthdays/anniversaries/holiday gift giving).

Decision catalysts: significant decisions delayed for internal reasons (sleep on it) or strategic timing (last responsible moment for best factor availability). He stresses that it’s OK “to decide not to decide” only if you have a decide-not-to-decide system.

Decision areas listed include: Hire/fire; Merge/acquire/sell/divest; Change job/career; Potential strategy redirection.

### The “Tickler” file (perpetual bring-forward system)
Tickler is a low-tech, three-dimensional calendar for physical reminders distributed so they automatically appear on their designated future date; it acts like a postal service for mail-to-self.

Alluded synonyms: “suspense,” “bring forward,” “perpetual,” “follow-up” file.

It can be supported by an assistant (e.g., “Hand me this agenda the morning of the day I have the meeting,” “Give this back to me on Monday to rethink,” “Remind me about the Hong Kong trip two weeks ahead…”), but Allen recommends maintaining your own tickler if possible.

Allen’s examples of use include travel documents needing a specific day, reminders of birthdays/special events that would take too much room on digital calendar, printouts for later exploration.

Operational requirement: tickler demands one-second-per-day new behavior (check and empty the next daily file), payoff grows exponentially because it represents the executive function “deciding not to decide until a certain point.”

#### Setting up a physical tickler
Needs **forty-three folders**: **thirty-one** labeled “1” through “31” and **twelve** month folders. Daily files sit in front beginning with tomorrow’s date; monthlies behind. Each day’s folder is emptied into in-tray and then refilled at back as perpetual. Monthly folder empties similarly to next year month.

Working advantage: can store actual documents needing future-day attention (forms, agendas, invoices held until that day).

Rules/caveats:
- must check/update every day;
- if you forget to empty the daily file, you won’t trust the system;
- if you leave town or don’t access on weekend, check folders for days you’re away first.

## Checklists: creative and constructive reminders
Checklists are external “recipes of potential ingredients” that provide check/review structure for projects/work/process/procedures/events/areas of value.

Allen links checklists to Whitehead’s observation: “Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.” Checklists provide micro support by entrusting details to your external mind.

He cites *The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right* (Alfred North Whitehead is quoted; The Checklist Manifesto is by Atul Gawande, with citation data: Metropolitan Books, 2009).

### Identify inherent projects/actions first
For “fuzzier” internal commitments, translate into projects/actions when possible:
- “Exercise more regularly” → “Set up regular exercise program” (project) + “Call Sally for suggestion about gyms and personal trainers” (action).
- “Maintain good morale on my team” → project like “Explore team-building processes for my department” + action like “E-mail our HR director to get her input on this opportunity.”

### When checklists are needed: blueprinting key areas
Some responsibilities don’t fit a direct project/action translation; they need overview checklists reviewed regularly. Allen references at least **six levels** of work, with examples of items in checklists:
- Career goals
- Service
- Family
- Relationships
- Community
- Health and energy
- Financial resources
- Creative expression

At the job layer, reminders might include:
- Team morale, Processes, Timelines, Staff issues, Workload, Communications, Technology.

Value sometimes is merely affirming “the area is OK as is,” but the checklist maintains relaxed focus.

### More novel situation → more control
Need for checklists depends on unfamiliarity with the area. When a procedure is unfamiliar (financial transaction steps, software login/refresh steps), you benefit from checklists. Allen notes being “dangerously semiliterate” for computers/software and creating checklists for IT instructions after repeated hard lessons.

Examples of situations needing temporary checklists: CEO disappears (fill her shoes); hired into new position; also Allen describes a personal temporary shift when launching a brand-new business structure, requiring checklists for accounting, computers, marketing, legal, and administration until “cruise control” returned.

### Checklists at all levels
Any checklist may be created ad hoc as needed. Allen suggests checklists include broad and specific topics, and provides many example checklist topics: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes, plus many others.

Operational advice: be ready to create and eliminate checklists; ensure new lists go to an easily accessed place (loose-leaf notebook or readily available software). Appropriately used, checklists enhance productivity and relieve mental pressure.

## Transition to next step
If you’ve captured open loops, clarified each in terms of meaning and required action, and organized everything into an intact system that provides current/comprehensive overview of present and someday projects, you’re ready for “the reflection process.”

He describes later questioning and skepticism: sneaking Nine Inch Nails T-shirts into Sunday school, reading Nietzsche, quitting Sunday school to smoke cigarettes, and a confirmation deal offered by a teacher (perfect marks if he stopped questioning Bible logic in front of other kids).

He reframes that what he resisted wasn’t torture but respect: dressing up signals seriousness to the community—virtue-signaling within the us-versus-them dynamic. He expands to robes as status cues, noting he first noticed them at college commencement (“hungover and on about three hours’ sleep”) and realizing he was “one of them.”

Mechanism: rituals exist because values must be lived/experienced, not “think[ed]…toward valuing.” Emotion is treated as action (“emotions are actions; the two are one and the same”), so to modify/reinforce the Feeling Brain’s value hierarchy, the religion needs “easily repeatable yet totally unique and identifiable action” that people perform. Rituals are repeated over long periods to amplify importance and provide symbolic narratives.

He gives examples of symbolism across contexts: churches with guys in robes dipping bread in wine and feeding it to represent the “body of Christ,” with symbolism tied to Christ’s sacrifice for salvation; countries create rituals around founding/wars via parades, flags, fireworks; couples create rituals/habits and inside jokes as reaffirmation of private interpersonal religion.

He claims ritual sacrifice (including ancient killings and “ripping out their still-beating hearts”) originally served guilt alleviation. He offers **Newton’s First Law of Emotion**: “every action produces an equal and opposite emotional reaction.” The wallet example triggers guilt because something good happens without deserving it. Then, existence itself triggers inherent guilt: you didn’t deserve existing; if you believe God gave it, you owe God; even if not, you’re “blessed with life,” raising “constant, yet unanswerable question of the human condition.” Spiritual religions use sacrifices to repay the debt; later symbolically sacrificing a life (e.g., “Jesus’s”) replaces repeated bloodshed.

He generalizes: most religious practices alleviate guilt; prayer is framed as “miniature episodes of guilt alleviation.” Ideological religions redirect guilt into service (“Our country gave you these opportunities, so put on a damn uniform and fight…” for right-wing; left-wing “giving up for the greater good of all society”).
