Manson describes the abusive feedback loop: promising salvation/enlightenment/world peace/perfect happiness yields follower underperformance; underperformance creates guilt; guilt drives obedience to “whatever you tell them to do to make up for it.” He compares it to pyramid schemes and claims that the seminar model psychs people up via chants and an us-versus-them dichotomy (“Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work for them!”) while still failing to teach how to sell. The key is blame transfer: instead of blaming the scam, followers blame themselves for failing to live up to their God Value.

He extends the same dynamic to fitness/diet plans, political activism, self-help seminars, financial planning, even visiting grandmother on a holiday—“the more you do it… the more you’re told you need to do it to finally experience” promised satisfaction that never arrives.

He then introduces the underlying reality: pain is a “game of Whac-A-Mole”—when you knock one pain down, another pops up; “it will always be there. It’s part of us.” He argues leaders stay in business by claiming they can solve the pain “once and for all,” but the game is rigged and blame is redirected to “you” or a nebulous “them.” If “them” were removed, it “just transfers the pain from one population to another, and amplifies it.”

He argues no full solution exists because no system can eliminate pain/inequality/fear/constraint: leaders need followers if things were perfect there’d be “no reason to follow anybody”; no country is “completely fair and safe”; true equality/true freedom are impossible; internal guilt cannot be absolved by anyone “no matter how much you love them.” The chapter’s conclusion of hopelessness is blunt: “It’s all fucked. Everything is fucked…There are no solutions, only stopgap measures…only slightly better forms of fuckedness.”

## Step Six: Prophet for Profit!
The final step makes religion a profit engine: the prophet reaps benefits from the devoted, with explicit mock fantasy examples (e.g., “Want a dozen sex slaves? Just say the word. Make up scripture…‘Stage Six of Manatee Enlightenment’ can only be found in the Prophet’s orgasms.”; “Want a huge piece of land…,” requiring followers pay; “Want power and prestige?” via getting voted into office or overthrowing government with violence; followers “give up their lives” for him).

He offers a systemic model: groups compete Darwinianly for “labor and capital”; religions that use value hierarchies most efficiently win and stabilize as culture. But success corrupts: when a religion spreads, its “God Value” shifts from original principles to “the preservation of the religion itself,” leading to organizational narcissism and historical corruption (he lists trajectories: “Jesus to the Crusades, Marxism to the gulags, from a wedding chapel to divorce court”). New reactionary religions rise when the original rots, and the cycle repeats.

Final caveat: “success” is precarious because more success means more to lose, harder to maintain hope; and, crucially, “the only thing that can ever truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.”

Kant is framed as simultaneously mechanically routine (waking 5, writing 3 hours, lecturing 4, lunch at the same restaurant, extended walks through the same park route leaving/returning at the same time, dinner with the same friend most evenings, bed at exactly 10 for forty years) and world-historical (inherent dignity grounding protections; idea of a global governing body inspiring the UN; space/time descriptions later inspiring Einstein’s relativity; early animal-rights suggestions; reinvented aesthetics/beauty; resolving rationalism vs empiricism; reinventing moral philosophy from top to bottom, overturning Western foundations since Aristotle).

Child psychology is driven by “Feeling Brains” collecting information on what pleases/harms, building an early value hierarchy and prioritization (the arc is hot stove → “really hot things suck,” ice cream in the freezer shelf → exploration/stealing). Punishment then teaches trade-offs (learning that “eating ice cream is better than being burned” but actions have competing consequences).

Exploration ends because there’s “too much world” to explore. Two brains shift toward rules to navigate complexity, adopted from parents/teachers and generalized (near open flames → all flames dangerous; raiding the freezer/freezer dessert → always bad). These rules become abstract; adolescents use if/then cause-effect reasoning rather than immediate impulse.

Adolescence still treats life as bargains, with pleasure/pain knowledge lingering but decisions becoming transactions made out of fear of negative repercussions (boss for money; calling mother to avoid yelling; homework to avoid fucking up the future; lying to avoid conflict). Values stay “self-defeating” because the adolescent never stands for something outside the self; relationships become manipulative means.

## Adult virtue: unconditional ends
“Doing adult things” can be rule/transaction-based (preventing childishness but not ensuring adulthood). Adult maturity is acting from abstract principles “for its own sake,” even when it hurts today or hurts others. Bargaining cannot generate love/companionship/respect/trust: if love must be convinced, it isn’t love; if respect requires cajoling, it isn’t respect; if trust is coerced, it isn’t trust. The most precious things are “by definition, nontransactional,” because bargaining destroys them.

Maturity depends on intentions, not age: child steals for how it feels; adolescent avoids stealing via a bargain with the future self; adult doesn’t steal because stealing is wrong and would feel worse about self even if she succeeds.

## Why we don’t grow
Transcendence beyond pleasure/pain comes through the pain of failure: good parenting uses correct consequences (punish stealing ice cream; reward sitting quietly in a restaurant) so children learn life’s impulses meet a rule-based world. Failing to teach this makes adult relearning socially painful (peers/society punish selfish disregard for others’ feelings and rules).

Abuse is a failure mode too: punishment follows no logical pattern, reinforces no deeper values, and is random/cruel, producing coping mechanisms instead of self-control; coddling can generate similar adult issues by leaving people stuck in childhood value systems.

Moving into adolescence requires trust that behavior yields predictable outcomes (stealing always creates bad outcomes; hot stove also creates bad outcomes). Without trustworthy institutions/leaders, stable rules/roles can’t form and decisions devolve into childish selfishness.

Trauma/neglect, especially bullying, can stall adolescence: victims assume affection/respect aren’t unconditional and must be earned via “canned actions” (dress/speak/act a certain way). Some become skilled at bargaining—charismatic manipulation that makes life feel like “one big high school gymnasium,” where you must shove before being shoved.

The remedy is teaching bargaining is a treadmill and meaning is achieved without conditions/transactions, mainly via example: show unconditionality by being unconditional; teach trust by trusting; respect by respecting; love by loving—without forcing these, since forcing makes them conditional.

Religions in “purest forms” use hope to pull toward unconditional virtues (unconditional forgiveness of Jesus Christ; Noble Eightfold Path; “perfect justice of Muhammad”). Enlightenment “ideological religion” shifts focus to measurable goals (greater happiness/less suffering; personal liberties/freedoms; compassion/empathy/equality) but fails because bargaining destroys happiness, enforcing freedom negates freedom, and creating equality undermines equality.

Kant is introduced as aware of the Whac-A-Mole game of maintaining hope against the Uncomfortable Truth: he despairs but refuses the conclusion that existence has no inherent value or that meaning is arbitrary story. Using the Thinking Brain, he deduces value without hope.

His starting observation: the only scarce/unique thing we can tell is present is consciousness. Humans can reason and, via reasoning plus will, improve and direct the world; we are sources of ingenuity/creativity, self-awareness, and (for all we know) intelligent self-organization. Thus the supreme value is the thing that conceives of value itself: the ability to form meaning. Consciousness is presented as the only force that can propagate itself—spreading intelligence and generating greater organization—so without rationality the universe would be waste, and without intelligence/freedom we might as well be rocks.

The fundamental duty is to preserve and grow consciousness in oneself and others—called “the Formula of Humanity”—expressed as: “Act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.”

Hope is framed as transactional (current actions for an imagined pleasant future). Transcending it requires unconditional action.

A burrito example distinguishes ends/means: eating the burrito is the end; driving/buying gas are means; if the wife’s happiness is the real end, then she is the end and the burrito is a means; if the wife’s happiness is only a means to sex, treating the wife merely as a means becomes “some shade of wrong.”

Wrong behavior is generalized as means/ends inversion: lying misleads another person’s conscious behavior to achieve the liar’s goal; cheating violates expectations of rational/sentient beings; violence uses another person as a means to political/personal ends.

Virtues are ends in themselves: honesty is good because it doesn’t treat people merely as means; courage is good because failing to act treats self/others as means to quelling fear; humility is good because blind certainty treats others as means to one’s ends.

## Day-to-day practice: respect self/world without heaven/hell
The Formula is explicitly “without hope”: no utopia, no hell, no superiority claim—only that conscious will is respected and protected. World improvement is framed as moment-by-moment self-improvement by choosing to treat self/others as ends.

Pleasure-driven self-satisfaction is treated as treating self as a means. Democracy is described as designed for average people being selfish/delusional, requiring interlocking systems so no one group can “completely hose the rest.” Because politics is transactional and power attracts corrupt/childish people, democracy enshrines adult virtues.

## AlphaZero: self-learning from scratch; fewer moves, total domination
In 2018 Google’s AlphaZero changes the premise: it’s programmed to learn games (not preprogrammed to play). Against Stockfish, AlphaZero can calculate 80,000 positions/sec vs Stockfish’s 70 million—likened to entering a footrace against a Formula One car—but it’s also “weirder” because on match day it had less than a day to learn chess from scratch, spending most of that time simulating chess against itself and learning via trial and error.

Despite this disadvantage, it wins overwhelmingly: in 100 games, AlphaZero won or drew every single game; “a mere nine hours” after learning the rules, it did not drop a single game. Peter Heine Nielsen is quoted: “I always wondered how it would be if a superior species landed on earth and showed us how they play chess. I feel now I know.”

After beating Stockfish, AlphaZero teaches itself Shogi (Japanese chess, sometimes argued more complex). It destroys Elmo: in 100 games it won ninety, lost eight, and drew two, while calculating far less (40,000 moves/sec vs Elmo’s 35 million), and again without prior Shogi knowledge.

The chapter closes by framing the “paradox of progress”: materially, things are arguably better, yet people feel more hopeless/anxious/desperate—“an irrational sense of hopelessness… spreading across the rich, developed world.”
It references books/authors making the “things are the best they’ve ever been and likely going to get even better” case: **Steven Pinker** and **Hans Rosling**, credited with many charts/graphs claiming uninterrupted progress and improved conditions.
But the chapter juxtaposes with multiple U.S./developed-world statistics:
- **Eighty-year** upswing in depression/anxiety symptoms among young people; **twenty-year** upswing among adults.22
- Since 1985, lower life satisfaction for men and women.24
- Stress levels rising over the past thirty years.25
- Opioid crisis: drug overdoses at an all-time high in the United States and Canada.26
- Loneliness/social isolation up: nearly half of Americans report feeling isolated/left out/alone.27
- Social trust plummeting: fewer people trust government/media/each other.28
- Social networks shrinking: in the 1980s, most common answer to how many people participants discussed important matters with in the prior six months was “three”; by **2006**, it was “zero.”29
It then asserts environmental/political risks: nuclear weapons access by “nutjobs,” growing extremism on right and left, and increasing popularity of conspiracy theorists, citizen militias, survivalists, and “preppers,” nearing mainstream.

A key paradox claim is stated explicitly: “the wealthier and safer the place you live, the more likely you are to commit suicide.”30

## Hope-building requirements and the chapter’s roadmap
The chapter argues hope must be aimed at the future, not solved problems/statistics. It claims hope doesn’t care about solved issues (gun deaths, car accidents, plane crashes, literacy in Mongolia—“well, unless you’re Mongolian”).31
To build and maintain hope, the chapter says we need **three things**:
1. **Sense of control** (felt ability to affect fate).
2. **Values** (something important worth striving for).
3. **Community** (group sharing values and working toward them).
Without community, values lose meaning; without values, nothing seems worth pursuing; without control, people feel powerless. Losing any of the three collapses the rest and hope.

- In 1954, Texas A&M was a men-only “cow college” whose campus “looked a little bit like a penitentiary.” Football coach Paul “Bear” Bryant took nearly 100 players to Junction (140 miles west of Austin) to “separate the quitters from the keepers.”
- The camp was demoralizing (“so sorry, that just looking at the place would discourage you”; “It wasn’t a football field, it wasn’t any kind of field”) and brutal—blistering heat, “one of the worst recorded droughts,” and a first-day full scrimmage where players were “throwing up all over the place.”
- Attrition was rapid: “Sixth Player Quits Team at Texas A&M” (Washington Post). After ten days, accounts put survivors at 27–35; “Nearly seventy players had quit.” Gene Stallings: “We went out there in two buses and came back in one.”

## Attribution doubts and why “toughness” doesn’t track
- A&M later improved (9–0 in 1956), but camp success is uncertain: only eight 1954 camp survivors played on the winning 1956 team because key freshmen didn’t travel (John David Crow, Jim Wright, Charlie Krueger). Ed Dudley: “Our freshman [in 1954] won the conference [in 1956].” Bryant also conceded the talent issue: “That first year was brutal… some of our alumni went out and paid a few boys,” and he notes better talent produced better results “regardless of how that talent was acquired.”
- Even if survivors “outlasted,” equating that with fortitude fails: quitters included future NFL player Fred Broussard and Joe Boring (switching to baseball and leading Aggies to a conference title). Foster “Tooter” Teague reportedly left due to injury, then became a Navy TOPGUN pilot (flew F-8 and F-4), earned a Silver Star, commanded USS Kitty Hawk, and was selected for a top-secret program to test a Soviet MiG.
- The camp’s real effect matched Bryant’s aim—eliminating players after a coaching regime change—but the chapter argues it “fundamentally failed” as a toughness developer for “the other two-thirds.”
- Bryant later apologized: “if it had been me, I’d have quit a dozen times, but they never quit. I didn’t know if I was doing it right or not, but it was the only way I knew how to do it.”

## The military lesson: teach coping capacity, then expose
- The military story is wrong as commonly told: boot camps don’t develop toughness; they risk mistaking sorting for development. The military prepares people to function under extreme stress.
- Under extreme stress, psychologists describe dissociation: detachment with amnesia, depersonalization, and derealization (an “extreme involuntary coping strategy, a last-ditch effort”). Research cited: 96% of soldiers report dissociative symptoms; 65% “lost track of what was going on”; “All but two of the ninety-four soldiers interviewed” felt “as if… through a fog.”
- Post–Korean War POW casualties shifted survival training to SERE (Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape), with three phases: classroom, evasion, detention. Key distinction: the classroom phase (“a barrage of lectures”) teaches coping skills; the AF SERE manual is “652 pages,” covering psychological issues (boredom, loneliness, hopelessness, losing the will to survive) and practical skills (camouflage, fire making, “river hydraulics”).
- Mechanism is stress inoculation: “vaccinate” against extreme stress by teaching coping skills first, then exposing—without overwhelming the system.

## From sorters to teachers: mental skills foundation
- Later military practice moved from physical difficulty to teaching: Bear Bryant–style camps were “great sorters but poor teachers.” In 1989, the US Military Academy created the Center for Enhanced Performance (goal setting, positive self-talk, stress management). As of 2018, the US Army employed the largest number of sports psychologists.
- A 2014 RAND review recommended emphasizing core performance skills (confidence, goal setting, attention control, arousal control, imagery, self-talk, compartmentalization, “mental skills foundation”) and mastering them before exposure (“teach the skill first”). Early 2000s Navy SEALs added a classroom phase to train candidates to “monitor their psychological performance.”

## Toughness reframed: coping skills under uncertainty
- Toughness isn’t eliminating discomfort; it’s maintaining function through uncertainty. Using the immune-system analogy: CSF aims to “maximize [a soldier’s] potential” to face sustained physical and psychological challenges, like building a robust “immune system.”

- Quitting thoughts are normal “mind-protection,” not weakness; Jonathan Wai: “I often side with the lower-hanging fruit.”

## Core cycle (preview)
- Sequence: **Feel → Inner debate → Urge → Decision (freak out OR find our way through)**; steps can blend, and exhaustion/anxiety increases reliance on the quick exit.
- The brain seeks closure by turning uncertainty into the known (quitting mid-project, changing expectations, or exploring/accepting/avoiding discomfort drivers). Toughness is training to handle uncertainty long enough to guide the “correct” response rather than the quickest one.

- Some can stay engaged and maintain cognitive wits during extreme stress; the goal is training that capacity so individuals can function when high stakes demand specific tasks.

- Survival training became strategic after mass POW casualties in the Korean War. In 1961 the Air Force opened its first survival school; Navy and Army followed; the SERE program (Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape) was born.

- SERE is grounded in stress inoculation: like vaccination, expose someone to extreme stress only after teaching coping skills; inoculation should not be so powerful that it “overwhelm[s] the system.”

- Later military learning: difficult tasks alone are insufficient; Bear Bryant–style boot camps are described as good sorters but “poor teachers.”
- In 1989, the US Military Academy introduced the Center for Enhanced Performance, focusing on goal setting, positive self-talk, and stress management; “mental skills coaching” spread across branches, culminating in nearly a dozen programs improving mental strength and resilience; as of 2018, the US Army is described as the largest employer of sports psychologists in the country.
- A 2014 RAND Corporation evaluation asked: “Is the Air Force doing everything it can to prepare battlefield airmen to perform successfully under stressful conditions?” Two top recommendation areas:
  1) emphasize core skills that aid performance (confidence, goal setting, attention control, arousal control, imagery, self-talk, compartmentalization, and mental skills foundation), and
  2) ensure those skills are mastered before stressful exposure (“teach the skill first”).
- Even the Navy SEALs recognized the distinction in the early 2000s by implementing a classroom phase to train candidates to “monitor their psychological performance and learn to maximize mental toughness skills.”

- Stress inoculation is said to work only with acquired skills; Brian Zuleger’s point is explicit: “Telling people to relax doesn’t work unless you’ve taught people how to actually relax… You have to teach the skill before it can be applied.”

- The chapter concludes that toughness isn’t an elimination or sorting exercise; it requires skillful navigation of adversity. Researchers evaluating soldiers who kept clarity under extreme stress found they:

## Marginal gains → identity via systems
In 2003 Dave Brailsford became performance director of British Cycling after “nearly one hundred years of mediocrity”; since 1908, British riders won just a single Olympic gold medal and none in the Tour de France, and a top bike manufacturer refused to sell bikes out of fear it would hurt sales.

Brailsford pursued “the aggregation of marginal gains,” improving “by 1 percent” across everything you can break down, so the total increase becomes “significant when you put them all together.” They made small, concrete adjustments (redesigned bike seats for comfort; rubbed alcohol on tires; electrically heated overshorts; biofeedback sensors; wind-tunnel testing of fabrics; switching outdoor riders to lighter, more aerodynamic indoor racing suits) and extended 1% gains into unexpected areas (massage gels to speed recovery; hiring a surgeon to teach hand-washing to reduce catching a cold; best pillow and mattress per rider; painting the inside of the truck white to spot dust that could degrade finely tuned bikes). Results came faster than expected.

## Compounding time produces lagging outcomes
Five years later, the team dominated Beijing 2008, winning 60 percent of available gold medals; in London they set nine Olympic records and seven world records. Bradley Wiggins became the first British cyclist to win the Tour de France; Chris Froome won next year and again in 2015, 2016, and 2017—five Tour wins in six years. From 2007–2017, British cyclists won 178 world championships, sixty-six Olympic or Paralympic gold medals, and captured five Tour victories.

Outcomes work as “a lagging measure”: net worth reflects financial habits, weight eating habits, knowledge learning habits, clutter cleaning habits—“You get what you repeat.” Time magnifies the margin: good habits make time “your ally,” bad habits “your enemy.”

## 1% change math: exponential, delayed breakthroughs
One defining moment is easy to overestimate; small daily improvements are often dismissed as unnoticeable. Yet 1 percent better each day for one year yields “thirty-seven times better,” while 1 percent worse declines “nearly down to zero.” Habits are “the compound interest of self-improvement.”

Progress is delayed because change isn’t linear: the “Plateau of Latent Potential” explains why people reach a “Valley of Disappointment” before an eventual shift is called an “overnight success.” Jacob Riis’s stonecutter quote (split in two at the hundred and first blow) supports the need for patience.

## Systems over goals: mechanics and problems
Goals are desired results; systems are the processes that produce them. Goals-first thinking causes four problems: (1) survivorship bias—winners and losers share the same goals; (2) achieving a goal is momentary unless the system changes (symptom vs cause); (3) goals restrict happiness by deferring it to milestones; (4) yo-yo after finishing—“The purpose of setting goals is to win... The purpose of building systems is to continue playing the game.” Goals can set direction, but systems are best for making progress.

## Atomic habits
Bad habits repeat because the system for change is wrong: “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.” An “atomic habit” is “a tiny change... a marginal gain, a 1 percent improvement” that functions as part of a larger system—small routines that compound like atoms building molecules toward “remarkable results.” If you want better results, “forget about setting goals. Focus on your system instead.”
